title: Too Good
passages:
The shackle was a seized pin in a rusted body, and it would have taken ten minutes with a hammer and a punch and a man who didn't mind losing skin. Sol didn't have ten minutes. She had the deck torch instead — a bottle of oxygen, a hose, and a steel pipe that burned a hole in anything you pointed it at — and she put the flame on the pin until the pin went white, then yellow, then let go, and six years of the Marrow tied to the transit station went down into the harbor in one long bright link at a time.

"You just set fire to six years," Wren said.

"I set fire to a pin." Sol killed the torch and racked it. "Six years is a number. Dey!"

Dey came up the deck with the axe. Twenty minutes out of the recompression box — the steel tube they'd pressurized to squeeze the fizz back into his blood — and he was still bent, still walking like a man on gravel in bare feet, and he took the axe off the rack and set his feet and knocked the last pinched link off the fairlead in two swings. Sparks went into the water and drowned.

"Show-off," Wren said.

"He's paid by the hour," Sol said. "Cast off."

The Marrow came off the station and swung her bow into the current, and Wren went to the storm glass for the number. The storm glass was a sealed tube of camphor and salt water that clouded as the air pressure dropped, so you could read the weather at arm's length instead of trusting a forecast. It had clouded two marks since dawn.

"Eight hours forty," she said.

"That's not nine."

"No. It's eight forty."

Sol said something about the Factor's mother that Wren chose not to put in the log.

"Course?"

"Zero-four-zero. The Mercy's bearing."

Sol took the wheel in both hands and held it like it owed her something. The Mercy General was six kilometers out, a hospital tower with its top nine floors in the air and the rest of it in the water, and the bearing to it ran across open chop the whole way. She pulled the grease pencil from behind her ear and wrote zero-four-zero on the back of her left hand, in the strip of skin below the thumb where she kept her numbers. There were older numbers there already, layered over each other in the same wax, some of them smudged to gray ghosts where her palm had dragged through them.

Wren looked at the old ones a beat too long. Sol put the hand in her jacket pocket.

"Log it," Sol said.

Wren logged it. Then she looked back at the glass, because the glass was where the argument lived, and the cloud had come up another mark while she stood there — a third of the tube gone white in the time it took to write a course.

"Eight hours forty," she said again, and heard how it sounded, and said it anyway.

Sol didn't look at the glass. She looked at the water ahead, and then at Dey, who had racked the axe and was standing at the rail with his weight on his heels like a man who'd forgotten he was hurt.

"Below," Sol said. "Both of you. I want the sled packed before we're in sight."

Dey went. Wren stayed one second longer at the glass, watching the white climb, and did the arithmetic she was going to have to do out loud in about four minutes, and hated every digit of it.

Below, the cabin was low and hot off the engine and crowded with everything the Marrow owned and never threw away. Dey had the suit to his waist already. Wren went to the bench, took his slate off its hook — a rubber-cased unit that logged his depth and his gas and ran the boat's voice into the bone of his jaw so topside could talk to him down there — and clamped it over the seal at his wrist.

"Give me your thumb," Dey said, and put his hand out, and she didn't take it.

On the slate's face was a line for the sign-off, the place where the topside tech certified a diver fit for the depth he was going to. Fifty-two. Her thumb had never once left that line blank.

"I'm not signing you," Wren said.

"For the case?"

"For any of it past forty." She turned the slate so he could see the empty line. "My thumb there says you're fit and it says I'll build you back if you're not, and I've done it a hundred times, and I'm not doing it to you at fifty-two."

"You did it to me yesterday."

"I cut you an hour yesterday and you kept the part I cut." She heard her own voice climb and didn't fix it. "That's the whole problem, Dey. It doesn't stay cut."

Sol came down the ladder, leaving the wheel to hold its own heading, into the middle of it. "Reader signs or Reader doesn't, we're on the Mercy in six hours. Pick."

"Then send me." Wren held the slate out like a warrant. "I'm rated to forty. I'll take the tether, I'll bring the case up, and he sits in the box where I can watch him."

"No." Sol didn't look at the slate.

"I'm the only one aboard who can put a man back together and you'd keep me on the bench—"

"That's exactly why." Sol took the slate out of her hand and hung it back on the hook, gentle, which was worse than if she'd thrown it. "You're the only one who can put him back. So you're the one stays dry. You go in the water and crack your head on a doorframe, then who builds him? Dey? You want Dey stitching a man's hours back with a boat manual?"

"I want Dey to have a man to stitch."

The engine filled the space where Sol didn't answer.

"You're not trading a case," Wren said, quieter, because quiet carried further down here. "Twelve thousand buys five berths on the high ground. I did the arithmetic — I do it every hour. You're not buying berths with the Factor's money. You're buying them with him." She pointed at Dey without looking, the way you point at weather. "You'll spend a nineteen-year-old's whole head for a dry bunk, and you'll do it because you can't remember you already spent your own the same way."

Sol's jaw worked. When she spoke it was even. "You cut Ivo Salas out of him and he kept it anyway. You've built every man on this crew back wrong on purpose so he'd sleep. Don't stand on my deck and price my trade when your whole job is deciding what people are allowed to know they did."

"Reader," Dey said.

Neither of them looked at him.

"I know what you cut," Dey said. "I kept it. Ivo lent me air at forty-two and he's still down there, and you both know it." He pulled the suit up over his shoulders and reached for the ring at his throat, unhurried, a man getting dressed for work. "So you can stand here and price each other, or one of you can come wind the winch."

He sealed the ring. The slate on his wrist chirped once, waiting for the thumbprint that would let him past forty, and Wren's hand was still empty, and above them the storm glass climbed another mark in the dark.

"Get the mix," Wren said.

Dey looked at the slate chirping on his wrist, then at her, and went forward.

He came back with the first bottle upright in both arms, bent at the waist, setting his feet down like a man crossing gravel barefoot, and walked it into the rack at the back of the sled. The sled was a welded steel skid about the size of a door: a cradle in the middle shaped to take the cold-case, a lifting ring at the nose for the tether, gas racked behind.

"White bands," Dey said, reading the shoulder. "Trimix."

"Oxygen, nitrogen, helium," Wren said. "Helium's so you don't get drunk at fifty-two. Oxygen's cut low so it doesn't burn you. Air would've been a fifth the price and you'd be a comedian on the bottom."

"I'm a comedian up here."

"You're a *dent* up here."

The second bottle went in beside the first. She read both gauges out loud, because a man ought to hear his own air before he trusts it in the dark.

"Three hundred bar each. Call it forty-one minutes of breathing. Thirty-eight if you dawdle, and you dawdle." She swung the rack bar down and dropped the pin through it. "There's no second set."

"No second set," Sol said from the ladder.

"Because the second set is twelve hundred and a berth is twenty-four hundred, and the Factor's advance went into these two and the diesel."

Overhead the deck chain went slack and started to rattle, and Sol came down with the green bottle in one hand, the mask still bagged and zip-tied to the valve, the clear hose coiled over her forearm.

She clamped it to the sled with two hose clamps and ran a lanyard through the ring, then stood back and looked at her work.

Wren stood up off the bench.

"That's the recompression bottle."

"It's reserve."

"It's oxygen under pressure on a full-face mask, two hours of it, and it's the reason he walked out of that box yesterday instead of being carried out." She kept her voice flat and clear, the voice she used for the log. "Say whose hide that's paid out of. Out loud. Slate's running."

Sol wiped her hands down her thighs. "Reserve is reserve."

"There's a steel tube in the lazarette with a hand pump and nothing to pump. He comes up bent, there is nothing on this boat that puts him back." Wren put her thumb flat on the slate's face — not the sign-off line, just the glass, over the count. "So you'd spend the one thing that would've, on a box."

"I'd spend it on five bunks."

"Then log it: one recompression bottle, out of Dey Okafor, twelve thousand."

"Log it as reserve gas."

"That's the same sentence with his name off it."

Dey took the other end of the green bottle before either of them could get a hand on it, and walked it forward, and set it in the clamps.

"Heavy for air," he said.

"It's not air."

"Nothing aboard this boat is what the label says." He threaded the lanyard, cinched it down, and patted the bottle twice, cheerful as a man loading groceries. "Forty-one minutes, Reader. I'll be up before you've finished being right."

Which was worse than if he'd argued.

She held out her hand and he gave her his wrist, and she keyed the cert line and put her thumb down and wrote *40* in the depth field.

Dey read it upside down. "That's not fifty-two."

"No. The slate alarms at whatever I certify, so above forty it stops telling me anything at all. I'll call your depth and your mix myself, every minute, by voice." She let go of his wrist. "Past forty you're off my log with nothing behind you but your word, and your word is what I'd have to build you out of."

"Fair," Dey said, and meant it, and that was the part she liked least.

She turned to lash the bottle down against the cradle, and the drone came down out of the chop and hung off the portlight, near enough that Wren could see herself in the lens, bent around the curve of it. It held there the whole time Dey sealed the second bottle, and then it went back up, unhurried, the way a thing goes when it has already counted what it came to count.

Wren watched it climb. Then she looked at the green bottle clamped where the treatment used to live, and at the empty bracket swinging on its chain over the deck.

"Thirty-eight," she said, to nobody, "if he dawdles."
